title: Build a money parser
prompt: Complete `parse_money(values)` so it takes a Series of text such as `" $1,234.50"`, `"$65.00"` or `"18.00"` and returns a Series of floats, turning anything unparseable (like `"N/A"`) into `NaN` instead of raising an error. Then replace `messy["total"]` with the parsed values, set `total_sum` to their sum rounded to 2 decimals, and set `over_200` to the number of rows with a total above 200.
hints: Inside the function: strip spaces, remove `$` and `,` with `.str.replace(..., regex=False)`, then convert.
`pd.to_numeric(cleaned, errors="coerce")` converts what it can and returns `NaN` for the rest.
Assign back with `messy["total"] = parse_money(messy["total"])`; count with `(messy["total"] > 200).sum()`.
explanation: The function removes the two symbols as plain text and lets `to_numeric` do the conversion, with `errors="coerce"` so a stray `N/A` becomes `NaN` rather than crashing the whole column. In this export every value parses (no new `NaN`s), which is what the `column-numeric` check confirms. `astype("string")` at the start is optional here but makes the function safe on a column pandas already read as numbers. The sum, 23,500.67, still double-counts nine duplicate rows; you fix that in Lesson 3.5.

checks.parse-basic: `parse_money` handles `$`, plain numbers and stray spaces
checks.column-numeric: `messy["total"]` is a float column with no failed conversions
